title: Bittul: dust and ashes
hookLine: setting the self aside to make room for the divine
carry: bittul: less of me, more room for god

cards: Abraham is arguing with God. Two cities are about to be destroyed, and Abraham, with nothing to bargain with, keeps pressing. What if there are fifty good people there?
He's bargaining with the Judge of all the earth. And right in the middle of that boldness, he stops and says something about himself.
In the old Jewish Publication Society translation, he calls himself one "who am but dust and ashes." Bold and small in the same breath.

teach.h: DUST AND ASHES. WHAT ARE WE?
teach.b: Bittul. Setting aside, making void, the self stepping out of the way. In Hasidic teaching, bittul is the practice of making less of yourself so there is room for God.
First, the two models. Abraham says he is dust and ashes. Moses, too, is remembered this way: the Torah says, "Now the man Moses was very meek."
And when the people complain, Moses and Aaron answer, in effect, what are we? The Talmud sets those sayings side by side, as if each is a step further into getting out of the way.
Second, it is not self-hatred. Abraham doesn't stop arguing because he's dust. He argues harder.
Moses is meek and leads a nation. Bittul isn't thinking you're worthless. It's not making yourself the center.
Third, the vessel. Hasidic teachers use the picture of a container.

teach.h: A CUP FULL OF ITSELF CAN'T RECEIVE.
teach.b: A cup already full to the brim has no space for what's being poured. Pour out a little of the self, and there's room.
That's why yesterday's teaching and this one fit together: the body can serve, and the self can step aside so the service is for God and not for show. Fourth, the everyday version.
Bittul can be as small as letting someone else's idea win in a meeting when theirs is better. Not mentioning your part in a success. Listening to the end of a sentence without preparing your reply.
Small acts of less me, so that something larger has room.

how: Hasidic teaching treats bittul as a lifelong practice of humility before God, cultivated in prayer and in ordinary dealings with others, and sees it as the ground of a person's service.

o: a fast day to atone for pride
a belief that you are worthless before God
setting the self aside to make room for God

s: bittul means believing you are worthless
Abraham calls himself dust and keeps arguing. bittul is not making yourself the center.
Abraham calls himself dust and ashes while bargaining with God
bold and small in the same breath.
in this teaching, a humble person has to stay silent
Moses is meek and leads a nation. stepping aside is not the same as stepping back from life.

games.q: you're Abraham. you've just called yourself dust and ashes before God. what do you do next?
o: fall silent, since dust has no right to speak.
keep pressing: what if there are fewer good people?
games.why: he keeps bargaining, fifty, forty-five, forty and on. his smallness doesn't silence him. it makes room for the plea.

practice: Notice how much of the inside of your head is about you, what to say, how you're coming across, what you're owed, and don't fight it; just notice its size.

Then, for a few breaths, set it down like a heavy bag, and let the room, the sounds and the people you love take up the space. If you pray, you can stand before God as Abraham did, bold and small at once.

wordCard.voice: Bittul. Setting the self aside to make room for the divine. Not self-hatred: an emptier cup, with room to receive. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: setting aside, making void. In Hasidism, the self stepping out of the way.

carryVoice: Your line: bittul: less of me, more room for god. An emptier cup has more room to receive what is poured. See you tomorrow.
